final_answer:
No, on the authority I could verify, the trial court did not err; disqualification was proper (and on mandamus review it should stand). Caveat: the full text of the key 2026 opinion could not be fetched (egress blocked), so its holdings are taken from search-result summaries of the opinion and not from the opinion itself.

Governing framework (Texas). Disqualification is a severe remedy, but Texas applies a special rule to side-switching nonlawyer staff. Under Phoenix Founders v. Marshall, 887 S.W.2d 831 (Tex. 1994), and In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010), a nonlawyer (paralegal/legal assistant) who worked on a matter for one side is conclusively presumed to have acquired the client's confidences. The presumption that the nonlawyer then shares them with the new firm is rebuttable, but only if the new firm shows it took prophylactic measures: (1) the employee was instructed not to work on the matter, and (2) the firm took other reasonable steps, in practice formal, institutionalized screening, to keep the employee off it. Disqualification is required if the nonlawyer in fact disclosed confidences, or if the firm failed to take those measures. In re Guaranty Insurance Services, 343 S.W.3d 130 (Tex. 2011), applies the same framework to staff who end up on opposite sides of the same matter. A simple informal admonition was held inadequate in Columbia Valley.

Application. Jones had substantive involvement on the Apex side: she prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications, and attended strategy meetings. So the conclusive presumption that she holds Apex's confidences applies. Her claimed lack of recall and the firm's assertion that she shared nothing do not rebut that presumption; the presumption is about what she acquired, and the rule does not turn on her present memory. Smith Fullingham then put her to work on the very matter, thirteen times over 2017-2022, and she e-filed two documents under her own name in March 2022. The firm did not ask about her prior work or instruct her not to work on the case, and it screened her only after Apex objected in January 2023. A screen erected after the nonlawyer has already worked on the matter, and after the conflict surfaced, does not satisfy the rule. The firm's 'limited secretarial work' argument fails, because the bright-line rule does not depend on the amount of work she did at the new firm.

In re Zaidi, No. 24-0245 (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026) (Devine, J.), is nearly identical on its facts (the real parties are Prestige/Turnaround Management Group; legal assistant who earlier worked for the opposing side; e-filing notifications). According to the summaries I found, the Court denied mandamus and held that a firm must admonish a nonlawyer not to work on any matter she handled at a prior employer at or before the time she begins work on a conflicted matter, even if the conflict arises years after hiring and even if she was not a side-switcher when hired. Not asking about prior work and not instructing her is not excused by the passage of time or the employee's hiatus from the workforce.

Waiver/delay. Waiver of a disqualification motion requires unreasonable delay after the movant knows the facts, and is judged by the circumstances (the relevant Texas cases, e.g., Vaughan v. Walther, were not independently retrieved). Apex learned of Jones's role in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023, about two months later, after inquiring of the firm. Per the summaries of Zaidi, the Court rejected waiver on similar facts, holding that e-filing notifications listing the assistant's name do not conclusively establish waiver as a matter of law. Apex's earlier receipt of filing notices bearing her name from 2022 (March 2022 filings) raises a possible constructive-knowledge argument, but it is the same argument Zaidi rejected as a matter of law; I could not verify the exact reasoning.

Bottom line: the firm cannot rebut the presumption: no admonition before she started on the matter, no formal screen, and she actually worked on the case, so the order was within the court's discretion and correct. Unresolved: I did not read the primary text of Zaidi, Columbia Valley, Phoenix Founders or Guaranty, so pinpoint holdings and any separate opinions are unverified.

claims.text: The trial court did not err in disqualifying Smith Fullingham.

A nonlawyer who substantively worked on a matter for one side is conclusively presumed to hold its confidences; the presumption of sharing is rebuttable only by timely instruction not to work on the matter plus reasonable screening.
Admonition must occur at or before the time the nonlawyer begins work on the conflicted matter, even if the conflict arises years after hiring; a post-objection screen does not cure.
Two months between learning of Jones's role and moving to disqualify, and earlier e-filing notices, do not establish waiver as a matter of law.
